headline: Acquisitions fuel sales surge but debt costs squeeze income
summary_short: Loar Holdings' Q1 FY2026 net sales rose 36.1% y/y to $156.1 million, boosted by the LMB and Harper Engineering acquisitions, but net income fell 27.2% y/y to $11.1 million as interest expense jumped to $18.7 million on debt taken on to fund those deals.
summary_long: Net sales grew 36.1% y/y ($41.4M), of which $28.4M came from the LMB and Harper Engineering acquisitions and $13.0M (11.4%) was organic, led by OEM commercial (+22.0%), aftermarket commercial (+14.1%) and non-aerospace (+46.4%) sales, partly offset by a 13.9% defense decline. Cost of sales rose to 49.2% of sales (from 47.9%) on acquisition-related inventory step-up and higher amortization. Operating income rose 28.2% y/y to $33.5M, but net income fell 27.2% to $11.1M as interest expense nearly tripled to $18.7M on acquisition-related borrowings. Cash rose to $94.9M; long-term debt rose to $950.1M after a $240M delayed-draw term loan drawdown for Harper Engineering. Outlook is qualitative only (organic growth plus acquisitions) with no numeric guidance given.

drivers.explanation: 36.1% y/y growth was driven $28.4M by the LMB and Harper Engineering acquisitions and $13.0M (11.4%) organically, led by higher OEM and aftermarket commercial demand and non-aerospace industrial gas-turbine components, partly offset by lower defense sales.

Cost of sales rose to 49.2% of net sales from 47.9%, primarily on inventory step-up recognized from the LMB and Harper Engineering acquisitions and higher intangible amortization, partly offset by operating leverage.
Interest expense rose $12.2M to $18.7M on acquisition-related borrowings, plus higher amortization and inventory step-up costs, which together outweighed the operating income gain.
The $2.5M y/y increase was primarily driven by higher noncash items included in net income, partially offset by an increase in working capital.
Company outlook anticipates continued net sales growth from organic backlog conversion and further acquisitions, with no material impact expected from inflation or supply-chain pressures.
